summary: Discusses the history and evolution of the Intermail and commercial mail systems and the problems of operating a store-and-forward mail relay between commercial systems such as Telemail, MCI Mail and Dialcom. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Different companies ran separate mail services. This tells how a go-between passed letters among them and what went wrong.

subtitle: Bridging electronic mail between the Internet and commercial systems.

tldr.problem: Internet users could not send email to people on commercial email systems like Telemail, MCI Mail, or Dialcom, creating isolated communication islands.
tldr.mechanism: Intermail and the Commercial Mail Relay (CMR) were developed as mail forwarding systems that translated between Internet and commercial mail formats, using store-and-forward relays to bridge the incompatible systems.
tldr.outcome: These services enabled cross-system communication for over a decade, proving that gateways between different mail systems were essential infrastructure.

today: RFC 1168 is an informational document describing experimental mail gateway services from the early days of Internet-commercial system interoperability. These specific systems are no longer in use, but the document is historically important: it shows how mail interoperability was achieved in an era of proprietary systems, and it demonstrates the need that later evolved into open standards like X.400 and modern internet messaging.

sections.title: The Problem: Isolated Mail Systems
sections.content:
In the 1980s, electronic mail had become a critical communications tool, but separate network systems used incompatible mail protocols and address formats. The Internet used SMTP-based mail, while commercial providers like Telemail (US Sprint), MCI Mail, and Dialcom each operated their own proprietary systems.

A researcher on the Internet had no way to send email to a colleague who had an account on MCI Mail. Similarly, someone using Telemail could not easily reach an Internet user. This fragmentation meant that organizations not directly connected to the Internet could not communicate electronically with the research community.

Intermail was developed at USC/Information Sciences Institute (ISI) to solve this problem. Beginning in 1981, it pioneered the concept of a mail forwarding gateway that could translate between incompatible systems and relay messages across system boundaries.
sections.eli5: Back then, different email companies used completely different systems, like post offices that couldn't deliver to each other. Intermail let a letter mailed one way be picked up and delivered another way.

sections.title: Evolution of the System
sections.content:
The original Intermail system was developed in 1981 on TOPS-20 computers to forward VLSI chip specifications between ARPANET and Telemail for the MOSIS project. It pioneered source route forwarding, an addressing method that specified the path a message should take through multiple networks.

As Intermail matured and gained acceptance, this approach was replaced with simple forwarding, a more user-friendly method where users could include address information at the beginning of their message body. This format supported special address types like U.S. postal addresses and TELEX numbers that Telemail could understand.

By 1988, the system was rewritten for UNIX as the Commercial Mail Relay (CMR), running on dedicated hardware using the MMDF (Multi-channel Memo Distribution Facility) mail software. The CMR was a more automated, production-grade system designed to handle large volumes of mail relay traffic between the Internet and commercial systems, supporting Telemail, Dialcom, and preparing to handle MCI Mail.
sections.eli5: The system started simple but grew more sophisticated. Each version made it easier for regular users to send mail across the systems without understanding all the technical details.

sections.title: How the CMR Works
sections.content:
The CMR operated as a store-and-forward relay, not a direct connection. Internet mail arriving on standard SMTP port was parsed and queued for the appropriate commercial system. Each commercial system had its own channel in MMDF, making it easy to manage separate queues.

For outbound mail, the CMR maintained relay mailboxes on each commercial system. Commercial users could send messages to the CMR mailbox using a Simple Forwarding Header (SFH) at the top of the message body. The SFH specified routing information like the destination Internet address, subject line overrides, and any carbon copies.

For example, a user on Dialcom could send mail to the CMR by addressing it to a relay account, prefixing the message with:

Forward: ARPA To: user@host.edu Subject: Meeting notes

The CMR would then route the message to the Internet user. Similarly, an Internet user could send to a commercial system by using syntax like [USER/ORG]SYSTEM/COUNTRY%SYSTEM@INTERMAIL.ISI.EDU.

The system supported automated error handling: messages with invalid addresses were automatically returned with explanatory errors, and the CMR's user-service mailbox (Intermail-Request@ISI.EDU) handled problems the software could not resolve.
sections.eli5: Mail came in one door, got translated to the right format, and went out another door. If something went wrong, the system tried to figure it out automatically before bothering a human.

sections.title: The Challenges of Translation
sections.content:
Bridging incompatible mail systems created many technical obstacles. The biggest was that commercial systems lacked machine-to-machine interfaces, forcing the CMR to mimic a human user—logging in, typing commands, and watching for responses. Any software change in a commercial system could break the CMR's parsing logic.

Address translation was particularly difficult. Internet syntax used formats like user@host.edu, while Telemail used [USER/ORG]HOST/COUNTRY and Dialcom used HOST:USER. Some characters used by commercial systems—like square brackets in Telemail addresses or colons in Dialcom—were problematic in Internet addressing and had to be quoted or worked around.

When Sprint migrated Telemail to X.400 addressing (a newer international standard), the CMR had to translate between old-style interconnect syntax and new X.400 syntax, adding another layer of complexity. The translation was not foolproof: different relays used different field names and values, requiring manual tweaking.

Another challenge was that commercial systems validated addresses slowly, often only after the entire message was transmitted. If a long message was sent to an invalid address, it wasted expensive connect time and was charged to ISI. Dialcom was better at this, validating addresses immediately.

Finally, the growing costs of connect time to commercial systems became the number one operational problem. The CMR had to keep working on ways to transmit faster: improving the current method, taking advantage of software changes, and upgrading modems and phone lines.
sections.eli5: Different systems used different languages, and sometimes they were hard to understand. Fixing a broken translation often took someone sitting down and figuring out exactly what the other system wanted.

sections.title: Who Used These Services?
sections.content:
Intermail and the CMR served diverse users. Scientists in oceanography, astronomy, geology, and agriculture used the services to communicate with colleagues who relied on Sciencenet (an Omnet service built on Telemail). The IEEE Computer Society used Dialcom's Compmail service for managing manuscript submissions and publication workflows, with authors on the Internet using the CMR to exchange large documents.

NASA used both Telemail for internal work and the CMR to communicate with university scientists. Government agencies like the National Science Foundation and USDA maintained dedicated group mailboxes on Dialcom. These services proved essential for institutional collaboration.

By 1990, other organizations had begun providing similar gateway services, including the Merit gateway to Sprintmail, CNRI's gateway to MCI Mail, Ohio State's gateway to Compuserve, and NASA-Ames' gateway to Telemail, demonstrating the widespread need for mail system interoperability.
sections.eli5: Everyone from NASA scientists to magazine editors used these relay services to stay in touch with people on different email systems.
